title: Impact of Elite High School Admission on SAT Scores

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)  

Why: Admission to the elite high school is determined solely by whether the student’s entrance‐exam score exceeds a known cutoff. Students just above and just below the threshold are assumed to be quasi-randomly assigned, so comparing their SAT scores identifies the causal effect of admission.  

Key assumptions  
1. Continuity: In the absence of admission, potential SAT scores are smooth in the admission-test score around the cutoff.  
2. No precise manipulation: Students cannot perfectly sort just above or below the cutoff.  
3. Sharp design: Treated = 1 iff running_var ≥ cutoff (verified in data).  

## 2. R Code
```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Impact of Elite High-School Admission on SAT Scores (RDD)
# -----------------------------------------------------------

# 0) Packages
required <- c("tidyverse", "rdrobust")
new_pkgs <- required[!(required %in% installed.packages()[,1])]
if(length(new_pkgs)) install.packages(new_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)

# 1) Read data
data_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s90_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(data_path, col_types = cols())

# 2) Inspect & set cutoff (verified by treated indicator)
cutoff <- 0.5                                # admission rule in the experiment
stopifnot(all(df$treated == as.integer(df$running_var >= cutoff)))

# 3) Main RDD estimate (local linear, MSE-optimal bandwidth)
main_rd <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$running_var, c = cutoff)

cat("\n--- Main RDD Estimate (Local Linear) ---\n")
print(main_rd)
cat("\nTreatment effect at cutoff =", round(main_rd$coef[1], 4),
    " (SE =", round(main_rd$se[1], 4), ")\n")

# 4) Basic robustness checks ---------------------------------

# (a) Tighter bandwidth: half of MSE-optimal
h_half <- main_rd$bws[1] / 2
rd_half <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, h = h_half)
cat("\n[Robustness] Half bandwidth (h =", round(h_half,3),") effect =",
    round(rd_half$coef[1],4), " (SE =", round(rd_half$se[1],4),")\n")

# (b) Quadratic polynomial
rd_quad <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, p = 2)
cat("[Robustness] Quadratic fit effect =",
    round(rd_quad$coef[1],4), " (SE =", round(rd_quad$se[1],4),")\n")

# (c) Donut RDD: drop observations extremely close to cutoff (|score-0.5|<0.01)
df_donut <- df %>% filter(abs(running_var - cutoff) >= 0.01)
rd_donut <- rdrobust(df_donut$y, df_donut$running_var, c = cutoff)
cat("[Robustness] Donut (exclude ±0.01) effect =",
    round(rd_donut$coef[1],4), " (SE =", round(rd_donut$se[1],4),")\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive. Students just above the cutoff (admitted) should score higher on the SAT than those just below the cutoff who were not admitted.  

Magnitude: Because SAT scores are standardized in the data (mean ≈ 0, SD ≈ 1), a reasonable local treatment effect is roughly +0.20 to +0.35 standard deviations—large enough to be educationally meaningful but consistent with prior literature on selective-school effects.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare SAT scores of students just above and below the admission cutoff.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Admission to the elite high school slightly decreases SAT scores.
